explanations: luna: The source section turns the sky above and earth below into a field-house; this verse joins earth as a resting place, sky as a canopy, rain, and fruit as provision. | terra: Earth is made a bed, sky a canopy, and water descends to bring fruit; this is the section's house becoming a field, with a watered ceiling and productive floor.

luna: The source section's dictionary gloss for ف ج ر is water opening in earth; here striking stone makes twelve springs gush, with water assigned to each group. | terra: Twelve springs burst from the struck stone and every people knows its drinking place, combining fajara-like opening with an apportioned share of water.
terra: The cow is described as neither trained to plough the earth nor water the field, a Quranic boundary image for the two human acts central to the section's cultivated ground.

luna: The source section explicitly connects water opening through rock to the field and to a heart made hard; this verse says rivers burst from some stones, giving the image its precise hard-surface reversal. | terra: Even stone can split so rivers burst from it, while the addressed hearts are harder; the section's opened watercourse becomes a test of whether the inner ground can yield.

luna: The source section uses rain and plant-growth to turn earth into a field; this sign passage links clouds, rain, rivers, and revived earth. | terra: Rain revives earth after death and the cloud is held between sky and earth, giving both cloud and water the life-producing role developed for sama.

luna: The source section opposes cultivated growth to burying and barren yield; this verse names a person who corrupts the land and destroys both harvest and offspring, showing growth being actively undone. | terra: The corrupter destroys crop and offspring, making moral corruption visible as the ruin of precisely what the section's purification-field should grow.
terra: Spouses are described as tilth and the addressees are told to send ahead for themselves, extending field imagery from crop growth to human generation and moral consequence.

luna: The source section's crop-growth gloss for ز ك و meets this image of one grain producing seven ears and multiplied harvest, making growth a figure for increase. | terra: A spent grain grows seven ears with a hundred grains each, giving the spending context of 2:264-265 its positive image of blessed multiplication.

luna: The source section contrasts growing soil with what produces nothing; here rain strips the thin soil from a stone and leaves it bare, a direct boundary to the fruitful garden in 2:265. | terra: Rain strips the thin soil from a smooth rock, showing exactly how the same water that nourishes a true field exposes ground incapable of growth.

luna: The source section turns sky and earth into a watered field; this hillside garden receives a downpour and gives double yield, showing what the same rain can nourish in receptive ground. | terra: Rain makes a high garden yield twice its fruit, directly staging the section's divinely blessed growth and contrasting the rock of 2:264.

luna: The source section evokes a watered home becoming a field; this garden has palms, vines, and streams, yet a fiery whirlwind burns it, the loss of cultivated growth. | terra: A fruitful, watered palm-and-grape garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind, completing the spending parables with cultivated abundance suddenly made fruitless.

luna: The source section's field yields growth from earth; this verse tells people to give from good things earned and grown from the earth, distinguishing sound produce from what one would reject. | terra: Believers are told to spend from the good things brought forth from earth and not select the bad, joining the spending parables' moral quality to the field's actual produce.

luna: The source section turns crop growth into a way to read moral increase; this verse says God erases usury and makes charitable giving grow, carrying the field's growth-versus-loss contrast into giving.
terra: Allah makes Mary grow with a beautiful growth and entrusts her to care, a direct human instance of the section's divinely nurtured plant-soul.
terra: Zechariah calls his wife عَاقِر, barren; the human use illuminates the section's lexicon of aqir sand as ground from which no life emerges.

luna: The source section's field depends on what nourishes it; this verse's cold wind strikes a people's crop and destroys it, showing the reverse of rain-fed growth. | terra: A freezing wind strikes and destroys the crop of people who wronged themselves, projecting inner wrongdoing as the loss of a field's growth.
terra: Allah knows every grain in the darknesses of the earth, illuminating the hidden seed-state from which the section distinguishes burial that prevents emergence.

luna: The source section follows ploughing with seed growth; this verse describes God splitting grain and seed-stones and bringing living from dead, the hidden opening that begins a crop. | terra: Allah splits grain and seed and brings living from dead, a non-irrigation formulation of the same opened-earth passage into growth.

luna: The source section makes rain and plant one field image; this verse sends water down and grows grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates from it. | terra: Water from the sky brings green growth, grain, palms, and gardens, and the command to watch fruit ripen displays nurture from emergence to completion.

luna: The source section's cultivated land yields crops and fruit; this verse names gardens, dates, vines, harvest, and the right owed from its produce. | terra: Gardens, palms, and varied crops bear fruit and have a due given at harvest, connecting divinely produced growth to an ethical share of its yield.

luna: The source section links cloud, rain, and a green carpet of plants; this verse sends a laden wind-driven cloud to dead land and revives earth with it. | terra: Before the good-and-bad soil comparison, heavy clouds carry rain to dead land and bring fruit; it supplies the watering scene whose different receptions 7:58 explains.

luna: The source section sets fertile land against sand that yields nothing; this verse contrasts good soil whose growth comes by its Lord's leave with foul soil yielding only scant growth. | terra: Good land yields vegetation by its Lord's permission while bad land yields only stunted growth; this is the section's two souls as fertile field and barren ground in one ayah.

luna: The source section ends its field account with the Thamud and the she-camel; this verse presents that camel as God's sign to the same people. | terra: Salih presents Allah's she-camel as a sign, lets her graze in Allah's earth, and forbids harm; this states the living boundary violated by aqr.
luna: The source section calls Thamud a people of the field; this continuation places them in the land's plains and describes their homes and settled use of it.

luna: The source section links ع ق ر to cutting a palm's growing head; this verse uses the root for the act against Salih's camel, the field's fruitful animal struck down. | terra: Thamud hamstring the she-camel and defy their messenger, preserving the exact aqr act whose secondary sense is cutting away the palm's growing crown.
terra: Faith and reverence would have opened blessings from sky and earth, while denial brings seizure; moral condition is expressed through the field's two sources.

luna: The source section glosses س ق ي through a measured drinking share; this verse gives each Israelite group its own known drinking place at the springs. | terra: Twelve springs issue from the rock and each tribe knows its drinking place, a direct communal parallel to the she-camel's protected water share.
terra: Charity is taken to cleanse and cause people to grow, linking the section's zakkaha to giving just as the rain-garden parables of 2:261-265 do.

luna: The source section's watered field is pictured flourishing and then failing: rain mingles with earth's growth until it is adorned, then a command leaves it cut down as though it had not flourished. | terra: Rain mingles with earth's plants until the land is adorned, then the crop is suddenly made as if harvested; growth and its removal expose the field's dependence.

luna: The source section calls Thamud a people of cultivated land; Salih reminds them that God brought them from earth and settled them in it, giving the land a human-growing sense. | terra: Salih tells Thamud that Allah produced them from the earth and settled them to cultivate it, identifying the camel-killers as a people raised in productive land.

luna: The source section connects the camel's water share with cultivated land; Salih tells Thamud to let her graze on God's earth and not harm her. | terra: Salih tells Thamud to let Allah's camel feed in His earth and not harm her, joining the cultivated earth of 11:61 to the act later called aqr.

luna: The source section's ع ق ر branch concerns cutting growth; this verse says Thamud hamstrung the camel after the warning about her grazing. | terra: After Thamud hamstring her, Salih gives them three days; this parallel keeps the aqr act inside the land-cultivation address of 11:61.
terra: Joseph commands seven years of diligent sowing and preservation of grain in its ears, presenting cultivation as foresighted care rather than guaranteed abundance.
terra: Seven severe years consume what was stored, placing a long barren interval against the preceding years of crop growth.
terra: A year of rain and pressing produce ends the drought, showing restored water returning a community to yield.

luna: The source section treats earth as the place where growth is spread; this verse describes earth extended with fruits and paired kinds, under day and night. | terra: Allah spreads the earth, places rivers in it, and makes fruits, bringing the section's spread surface and cleaving waterways into one productive landscape.

luna: The source section contrasts good land with land that scarcely yields; here adjoining plots receive the same water yet differ in their produce. | terra: Adjacent plots, vines, crops, and palms receive the same water yet differ in fruit, sharpening the section's claim that water alone does not make every inner ground alike.

luna: The source section names river-cut earth and water channels on slopes; this verse's valleys carry water in measured quantities, a specific picture of channels directing water through land. | terra: Rain makes valleys flow according to their measure; the measured watercourses concretize the section's hillside channels and apportioned irrigation.

luna: The source section's crop roots into soil and multiplies; this verse's good tree has a firm root and a high branch, making rootedness the condition for growth. | terra: A good word is a good tree with a firm root and branches in the sky, giving the section's rooted, upward growth a moral form.

luna: The source section describes growth that continues through blessing; this tree gives fruit at every season by its Lord's permission. | terra: The good tree gives fruit continually by its Lord's permission, joining mature yield to the same divine permission named for good soil in 7:58.

luna: The source section opposes rooted growth to what is buried and cannot sprout; this bad tree is uprooted and has no stability. | terra: The bad word is an uprooted tree with no stability, the moral reverse of a soul that takes root and multiplies like the section's fertile plant.

luna: The source section joins rain and land to provision; this verse names rain, fruit, rivers, and ships among God's provision. | terra: Water from the sky brings fruit and rivers are subjected, joining rain, produce, and running channels within one provision scene.

luna: The source section sets fruitful earth against ground that grows nothing; Abraham names a valley without cultivation and asks God to provide fruit there, making provision answer the barren landscape.

luna: The source section's field image depends on earth made productive; this verse spreads earth and grows things in measured balance. | terra: The earth is spread out and every well-balanced thing is made to grow in it, directly pairing the section's spread ground with measured fertility.
luna: The source section links the soil's growth to provision; this verse says livelihood is placed in earth for people and other creatures.
terra: Every created provision has known measure and descends only in measure, clarifying why the field's water is a share rather than an owned source.

luna: The source section describes opened watercourses and a field's water share; this verse sends fertilizing winds and water down from the sky to drink. | terra: Fertilizing winds are sent and water descends from the sky for people to drink, while they do not store its source; the field's growth and water remain divine provision.

luna: The source section calls the sky rain and plant in its dictionary account; here water comes from the sky and supports drink, trees, and pasture. | terra: Water descends from the sky for drink and for vegetation on which animals graze, matching sama as rain and plant-provider.

luna: The source section describes a watered, spreading crop; this verse explicitly says water grows grain, olives, palms, and grapes. | terra: The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit, expanding the section's green floor into its full produce.

luna: The source section invokes 16:59's burial of a girl in soil; this preceding verse gives the disgrace and concealment that lead into that burial, though it does not itself describe earth or growth.

luna: The source section says دَسَّىٰهَا evokes pressing into earth and opposes ز ك و growth; this verse's question about burying a girl in dust gives the literal scene and its moral reversal. | terra: The ashamed father considers pushing the girl into the dust, the Quranic yedussuhu scene that the section uses for burial too deep for growth.

luna: The source section's root ز ك و names growth and blessing; this verse makes rain revive dead earth a sign for those who listen. | terra: Rain revives earth after its death, a concise recurring formulation of the passage from non-growing ground to living soil.
terra: A secure town receives abundant provision and then tastes hunger after ingratitude, translating the fertile field's moral dependence into communal provision and its withdrawal.
terra: The prayer recalls parents raising the child when small; this is the Quranic human instance of tarbiya as bringing something stage by stage toward maturity.

luna: The source section defines the dictionary form الفجرة as a place where water opens; this verse's demanded spring bursting from earth is a direct water-opening scene. | terra: The demanded sign is a spring made to gush from earth, isolating the same water-opening action that 17:91 places inside a garden.

luna: The source section defines ف ج ر through water opening; this verse asks for a garden of dates and grapes with rivers gushing through it, joining the field and opened watercourse. | terra: A garden of palms and grapes with rivers made to gush abundantly through it directly joins mature cultivation to the section's fajara water-opening.
terra: Allah will make earth's present adornment into barren dust, a direct terminus opposite the section's green, carpeted surface.

luna: The source section's field becomes garden through water and cultivation; this verse stages two grape gardens ringed by palms and crops. | terra: The parable's two grape gardens, palms, and intervening crop present a deliberately ordered, productive field.

luna: The source section describes the crop reaching growth; this continuation says both gardens yield their fruit and a river runs between them. | terra: Both gardens yield fully and a river is made to gush between them, directly combining complete fruiting with the section's opened watercourse.
terra: The garden's owner possesses abundant fruit and boasts of wealth, beginning the passage's exposure of a soul corrupted by gifted yield.
terra: He enters his garden while wronging himself, explicitly placing the state of the nafs inside the cultivated landscape.
terra: He assumes the garden will never perish and doubts the final return, mistaking contingent growth for permanent possession.
terra: His companion recalls human creation from dust and then a drop, returning the proud cultivator himself to earthly, dependent beginnings.
terra: The believing companion names Allah as his Lord and refuses partners, identifying the true Rabb behind the garden's nurture.
terra: The garden owner should have acknowledged Allah's will and that power belongs to Him; this states the divine dependence of the section's apparently human cultivation.
terra: A calamity from the sky can turn the proud garden into bare, slippery ground, reversing the section's rain-from-above into exposed infertility.

luna: The source section names waterways in slopes and a land's water share; this verse warns that the garden's water could sink into the earth and become inaccessible. | terra: The garden's water may sink beyond recovery, defining the boundary of cultivation when its hidden watercourse is withdrawn.

luna: The source section contrasts cultivated yield with barren ground; this garden is ruined until its owner turns his hands over what he spent and sees it collapsed. | terra: The garden's fruit is encompassed and its trellises collapse, showing the completed crop undone when its owner mistakes gifted growth for possession.

luna: The source section sets flourishing soil against sand that yields nothing; here rain-fed vegetation turns to dry fragments scattered by wind, showing growth's passing. | terra: Worldly life is likened to rain from the sky whose vegetation mingles with the earth and then becomes wind-scattered stubble, a complete growth-and-loss version of the section's field.
terra: Zechariah's wife is again called barren, making عَاقِر a direct reproductive counterpart to the section's sterile sand.
terra: The repeated description of the wife as عَاقِر reinforces the root's boundary between capacity for growth and apparent incapacity.
terra: A stream is placed below Mary beside the palm, bringing water to the place where fruit will be received.
terra: Shaking the palm brings fresh ripe dates down, a compact scene of mature palm yield supported by the nearby stream.

luna: The source section says the dwelling's roof and floor become a field; this verse describes earth as a bed, paths through it, and rain bringing out varied plants. | terra: Earth is made a bed, paths opened, water sent from the sky, and diverse plants brought forth, nearly reproducing the section's entire house-field sequence.
terra: Humans are created from earth, returned into it, and brought out again; this distinguishes burial that leads to emergence from the section's smothering dassa.
terra: The believer who does righteous deeds receives the highest ranks; this identifies the cultivated moral life whose watered-garden reward 20:76 names.

luna: The source section explicitly reads تزكى through the root's growth and blessing; this verse places that growth-word beside gardens with rivers as the reward. | terra: Gardens with rivers beneath are declared the reward of one who tazakka, joining purification-growth to the fully watered field exactly as the section does.
terra: The levelled earth becomes a smooth bare plain, an eschatological counterpart to the section's ground on which nothing can take root or grow.
terra: All living things are made from water after heaven and earth are parted; this supplies the cosmic premise beneath the section's water-enabled growth.

luna: The source section's dry, unproductive land has its reversal here: dead earth stirs, swells, and grows every beautiful kind, alongside human formation from earth. | terra: Lifeless, barren earth stirs, swells, and grows every lovely kind after rain; it precisely crosses the section's boundary between sterile ground and living field.

luna: The source section pictures sky-water spreading life over earth; here rain makes the earth green, so the field's change is visible. | terra: Water descends from the sky and the earth becomes green, directly condensing the section's ceiling-water and living-floor image.
luna: The source section glosses أَفْلَحَ through ف ل ح, the farmer who splits earth; this verse uses the same verb for believers' success, letting the field-work sense illuminate flourishing.

luna: The source section's soil has a water share; this verse says water is settled in earth but can also be taken away. | terra: Water is sent down in due measure and lodged in the earth, with an explicit warning that it can be removed; this clarifies the field's allotted drink and its dependence.

luna: The source section describes a home turned into field; this verse grows gardens of palms and grapes with abundant fruit for eating. | terra: That measured water produces palm and grape gardens with abundant fruit, the mature outcome of the section's apportioned irrigation.
terra: The measured rain and gardens of 23:18-19 continue in a tree from Sinai yielding oil and food, another mature product of divinely watered growth.
terra: Allah purifies whom He wills, supplying the theological limit to the field image: the soul's growth, like the crop's, depends on divine action.
terra: Clouds are driven, joined, and piled before rain emerges, detailing the cloud-to-rain process compressed into the section's extended meaning of sama.

luna: The source section links sky-water and land-growth; this verse describes pure water sent from above before the dead-town revival in 25:49. | terra: Winds announce mercy and pure water descends from the sky, presenting the nourishing cloud-water aspect of sama.

luna: The source section's cloud and rain nourish the field; this verse says rain revives a dead town and waters animals and people. | terra: That water revives dead land and waters livestock and people, joining land's life with the distribution of drink.

luna: The source section shows land becoming a planted field; this verse asks how many noble pairs of growth have been brought forth from earth. | terra: The command to look at earth and the many noble pairs made to grow there directs the reader to the same divine husbandry as the section.
terra: Pharaoh claims to have raised Moses as a child; his boast supplies a contrary human claim to the nurturing action that the section locates in Rabb.
terra: The question whether Thamud will be left secure amid what surrounds them introduces the gardens, springs, crops, and palms of 26:147-148 as vulnerable gifts.

luna: The source section says Thamud lived amid cultivated land; this verse names their gardens and springs. | terra: Thamud's gardens and springs supply the fertile, watered setting in which the section hears their crime against the she-camel.

luna: The source section identifies Thamud with fields and palms; this adjacent verse names their crops and palms with tender fruit, specifying the cultivated abundance around them. | terra: Thamud live among crops and tender date-palm spathes; the thriving palm makes their act of aqr, also used for cutting a palm's crown, especially pointed.

luna: The source section glosses س ق ي as a land's allotted share of drinking water; this verse gives the she-camel and people separate, appointed drinking turns. | terra: Salih states that the she-camel has one drink and the people another on an appointed day, explicitly spelling out the suqya whose violation 91 recalls.

luna: The source section describes Thamud's water allotment and the she-camel; this continuation forbids harming her and completes the water-share warning. | terra: Salih's prohibition against harming the she-camel marks the boundary immediately before Thamud perform aqr in 26:157.

luna: The source section's ع ق ر dictionary branch is cutting a palm's growth point; this verse says they hamstrung the camel and regretted it. | terra: Thamud hamstring the camel and then regret it, repeating the section's action of cutting off life in a people surrounded by crops and palms.
luna: The source section joins Thamud's act against the camel to the Lord's response; this continuation supplies the punishment that follows their slaughter.

luna: The source section turns the sky's water into a cultivated ground; this verse asks who grows beautiful gardens by rain and makes their rivers flow. | terra: The question who sends rain and grows splendid gardens answers the section's agricultural acts by locating growth with Allah.
luna: The source section pictures water opening and moving through cultivated land; following the gardens in 27:60, this verse contributes fixed earth, rivers, and barriers between waters.
terra: Rain from the sky revives dead earth, restating the section's fertile/barren boundary as an acknowledged act of Allah.
terra: Allah brings living from dead and revives earth after its death, supporting the section's use of plant growth to make the living soul perceptible.
terra: Rain descends and revives earth after death, while lightning holds fear and hope; water can be awaited as the field's uncertain life.
luna: The source section identifies the root ز ك و with growth arising from God's blessing; this verse contrasts increase sought through usury with zakah given for God's sake and multiplied by Him.

luna: The source section names cloud, rain, and plant as one field system; this verse follows winds lifting clouds until rain emerges from them. | terra: Winds raise and spread cloud, then rain is seen emerging, detailing how the section's sky-cloud supplies water to earth.
luna: The source section depicts rain as the field's nourishment; this verse describes people's despair before rain arrives, completing the cloud scene in 30:48.

luna: The source section makes soil's growth visible; this verse directs the reader to the signs of mercy in how God revives earth after its death. | terra: The hearer is told to look at the traces of mercy in earth revived after death, turning the watered field into a sign of restored life.
terra: After the rain-and-revival sequence, a wind can leave the crop yellow and provoke ingratitude; it reverses the nurturing cloud into failed growth.

luna: The source section's field is earth watered from above; this verse explicitly connects rain with growing every noble kind of plant. | terra: Water from the sky causes every noble kind to grow in earth, directly joining the spread land to divinely supplied fertility.

luna: The source section's field is watered to produce growth; this verse brings water to barren land and grows crops for people and their livestock. | terra: Water is driven to barren land and crops emerge for livestock and people, directly showing sterile ground made productive by routed water.

luna: The source section presents land whose plants sustain a people; Sheba's two gardens furnish food and a call to gratitude from the Lord. | terra: Saba's two gardens and command to eat their Lord's provision stage fertile land as a sign requiring gratitude.

luna: The source section names sand that grows nothing; after the people turn away, their gardens are replaced by bitter, sparse growth. | terra: After Saba turns away, the flood replaces their two gardens with bitter fruit, tamarisk, and sparse lote trees; managed fertility becomes meagre growth.
terra: The ruined gardens are named repayment for ingratitude, explaining why the fertile land of 34:15 becomes poor growth in 34:16.

luna: The source section traces nourishment from cloud to ground; this verse drives a cloud to dead land and revives earth with rain. | terra: Winds raise cloud, which is driven to dead land and revives it; the named cloud performs the nurturing work the section hears in Rabb.
terra: Whoever purifies does so for his own soul, making the section's cultivation reflexive: the yield returns to the ground being cultivated.
terra: Water from the sky produces fruits of differing colours, adding visible variety to the section's single principle of blessed growth.

luna: The source section's ground is split and made to yield; this verse calls dead earth a sign and says grain is brought out of it. | terra: Dead earth is revived and grain is brought from it for people to eat, an exact reversal of the section's sand that grows nothing.

luna: The source section describes soil watered into growth; this verse places date and grape gardens and springs in that revived land. | terra: Palm and grape gardens are furnished with bursting springs, joining the section's fajara water-opening to productive land.

luna: The source section asks what the field produces; this verse points to fruit for people to eat, a provision they did not make grow by their own hands. | terra: People eat the field's fruit though their hands did not create it, reinforcing the section's attribution of growth to the Lord's blessing.
terra: Allah causes a broad-leaved plant to grow over Jonah, a small human-and-plant scene in which divinely supplied growth shelters a recovering person.

luna: The source section joins rain to crop growth; this verse traces water through the earth to varied crops, then their yellowing and reduction to debris. | terra: Water from the sky is conducted as springs through the earth and produces varied crops, directly joining watercourses, irrigation, and growth before the crop withers.

luna: The source section's irrigated earth spreads into growth; this verse says barren ground stirs and swells when water reaches it. | terra: Humbled, lifeless earth stirs and swells when water descends, a precise revival of the section's non-growing ground.
terra: The one seeking the harvest of the Hereafter receives increase in that harvest, while the worldly harvest is limited; cultivation becomes a measure of what the soul grows toward.
terra: Rain descends after people despair and divine mercy is spread, making water's arrival the reversal of an apparently hopeless dry condition.

luna: The source section describes rain reaching soil and growth; this verse says water descends by measure and spreads life through a dead town. | terra: Measured water descends from the sky and revives a dead land, combining the field's allotted water with its passage from barrenness to growth.
terra: Provision descends from the sky and revives earth after death, using the rain-fed field as a sign for those who reason.
terra: Aad see a cloud approaching their valleys and expect rain, but it is the punishment they hastened; the apparent nurturing cloud carries the opposite outcome.
terra: The wind destroys by its Lord's command until only dwellings remain visible, completing the reversal of hoped-for rain into a land emptied of life.
terra: Believers are likened to a crop whose shoot emerges, strengthens, thickens, and stands on its stem, a full moral enactment of gradual plant-like nurture.

luna: The source section describes the earth spread as a field; this verse pairs that spread with mountains and every beautiful kind of growth. | terra: Earth is spread out and every beautiful pair is made to grow in it, explicitly combining the section's laid-out surface with fertility.

luna: The source section follows water opening through soil into growth; this verse names blessed rain growing gardens and harvest grain. | terra: Blessed water descends from the sky and grows gardens and harvested grain, directly uniting sama, blessing, and crop growth.

luna: The source section names palms among the people of Thamud; this verse shows tall palms with clustered fruit as a sign of provision. | terra: Lofty palms with layered fruit clusters give the mature palm image whose growing point the section says aqr can destroy.

luna: The source section links crop growth to provision; this verse says the rain-grown yield is sustenance for servants and revives a dead town. | terra: The crop is provision and the rain revives dead land, making the fertile/barren contrast also an image of human emergence.
terra: Earth splits away from people as they hasten out, turning the cracked-ground image into human emergence and extending the human-as-plant analogy to resurrection.
terra: Abraham's wife calls herself barren with عَقِيم, a different root whose infertility still parallels the section's secondary image of sand incapable of producing life.
terra: The wind sent against Aad is called barren, a wind that bears no nourishing rain and thus reverses the fertilizing winds and fertile ground of the section.
terra: The barren wind leaves everything it reaches like decayed matter, giving the destructive yield of the sterile force named in 51:41.

luna: The source section's root ط ح و describes plant spread over earth's face; this verse describes earth laid out as a bed, the surface on which that carpet lies. | terra: Allah spreads earth and names Himself its excellent preparer, supporting the section's sense of a surface made fit to receive growth.
terra: Humans are known from their emergence from earth and are told not to declare themselves pure, joining earthen origin to a warning against claiming one's own growth.
terra: The gates of the sky open with pouring water; this reverses the nurturing ceiling-water image into the flood that destroys.

luna: The source section's root ف ج ر names the place water opens; this verse has earth opening into springs, an exact landscape counterpart. | terra: Earth is made to burst into springs and the two waters meet for a decreed matter, turning the section's opened irrigation channels into an overwhelming judgment.

luna: The source section's date-palm dictionary branch concerns cutting its crown; this verse likens the ruined people to uprooted palm trunks. | terra: People are torn away like uprooted palm trunks, turning the section's plant-like human growth into the image of a people violently removed from their roots.

luna: The source section links the she-camel's water share to the Thamud's test; this verse calls the camel a trial, completed by the water division in 54:28. | terra: The she-camel is sent as a trial and the prophet is told to watch patiently, introducing the apportioned-water command of 54:28 and the aqr of 54:29.

luna: The source section treats سُقْيَا as the camel's water share; this verse explicitly orders that the water be divided between them. | terra: The water is declared divided between Thamud and the she-camel, with each turn attended; it is the clearest parallel for the section's field-water allotment.

luna: The source section connects ع ق ر with cutting the growing point of a palm; here the same act-root names the killing of the she-camel whose water was shared. | terra: They summon their companion, who takes hold and hamstrings the camel; the compact scene directly preserves the root عقر.
luna: The source section links the she-camel's killing to the field's destruction; this continuation asks how the warning and punishment came after the act.
luna: The source section sets fruitful palms against barren land; after the camel is killed, the people become like dry palm stumps or gathered stubble.

luna: The source section treats earth as a field laid open for growth; this verse says earth is set out for living creatures. | terra: Earth is laid out for creatures, establishing the spread floor that the following two ayat fill with produce.

luna: The source section's cultivated field yields fruit; this verse names fruit and date palms among the earth's provision. | terra: Fruit and palms with sheathed clusters occupy that laid-out earth, showing its mature yield.

luna: The source section depicts growing crops; this verse names grain with husk and fragrant plants as earth's yield. | terra: Husked grain and fragrant plants complete the spread-earth sequence as a cultivated and provision-bearing surface.

luna: The source section treats cultivation as the work behind أَفْلَحَ; this verse asks the reader to look at what people plough, opening a direct agricultural counterpart. | terra: The divine question directs attention to what people till, isolating the human act of cleaving the soil that the section finds in falaha.

luna: The source section reads ز ك و as the crop's growing; this verse asks who makes the sown crop grow, locating growth with God. | terra: The question whether people make the crop grow or Allah does states the section's distinction between human ploughing and growth granted by divine blessing.

luna: The source section's barren sand and buried seed mark growth's opposite; this verse says a crop could instead be made into dry debris. | terra: Allah could make the crop broken debris, setting the barren possibility beside the claim in 56:64 that He is its true grower.

luna: The source section asks what becomes fit to grow; this continuation records the cultivators' loss after the crop is ruined, the human consequence of failed yield. | terra: The cultivators would be left lamenting their loss, exposing human labour's inability to secure growth.
luna: The source section contrasts fertile growth with nothing yielding; this continuation names deprivation after the crop's loss.
terra: The command to consider the water people drink begins the second half of the same field lesson: the cultivator does not originate the field's water.
terra: The question whether people bring water from the raincloud or Allah does directly matches the section's sama as cloud and rain that nurtures growth.
terra: Allah could make rainwater bitter, marking the boundary between water's mere presence and its fitness to nourish a field.
terra: Allah's reviving of earth after its death is offered as a clarified sign, supporting the section's moral use of fertile and dead ground.
terra: Rain-fed vegetation delights its cultivators, then yellows and becomes debris; the field renders visible growth that does not remain.

luna: The source section's dictionary form عَقَرْت النخلة describes cutting a palm's growing crown; this verse speaks of cutting palm trees or leaving them standing, giving that destructive agricultural act a Qur'anic scene. | terra: Some palms are cut down and others left standing on their roots, a Quranic boundary scene for the section's secondary sense of aqr as destroying a palm at its growing crown.
terra: If water sinks away, no one can bring flowing water; the question exposes how quickly an irrigable field can become the section's sterile ground.

luna: The source section's image centers on land cultivated for growth; this verse begins a garden story with owners who expect its harvest. | terra: The owners of a garden are tested when they swear to harvest it in the morning, beginning a parable of presumed control over cultivated yield.
terra: The garden owners make no exception to their harvest resolve, leaving their plan unqualified and setting up the exposure of assumed control over yield.
terra: A visitation from the Lord circles the garden at night while its owners sleep, locating the field's fate beyond their labour.

luna: The source section contrasts growth with land that yields nothing; the garden becomes كَالصَّرِيمِ, which can mean darkened or reaped, so the cut-field reading recalls the image but remains uncertain. | terra: By morning the garden is like a field already stripped bare, the sudden sterile reverse of growth expected for harvest.
terra: They urge one another to go early to their crop if they intend to harvest, keeping the destroyed garden explicitly within cultivated labour.
terra: They plan that no poor person enter the garden, showing the moral barrenness accompanying their intended harvest.

luna: The source section traces what a field can yield or lose; after seeing the ruined garden, its owners recognize they were deprived. | terra: On seeing the ruined garden they recognize themselves as deprived, naming the loss of yield their confidence had denied.
terra: The most balanced among them recalls having urged glorification, shifting the failed field toward recognition of its Lord.
terra: They glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, making repentance the first inner growth produced by the barren garden.
terra: They hope their Lord will replace the garden with a better one, reopening the possibility of growth under acknowledged divine nurture.
terra: Aad lie like hollow, fallen palm trunks after the wind, another precise reversal of humans flourishing as plants.

luna: The source section joins sky, rain, and a growing field; this verse promises abundant rain, followed immediately by gardens and rivers in 71:12. | terra: Noah promises abundant rain from the sky, supplying the water for the human-plant image later stated in 71:17.

luna: The source section says the self is grown like a plant and links the Lord to nurture; this verse joins rain with gardens and rivers as gifts. | terra: That rain is joined to gardens and rivers as divine increase, linking human multiplication with the growth of a watered field.

luna: The source section says the nafs grows like a field; this verse makes the human being itself a plant grown from earth, joining moral growth to cultivation. | terra: Allah causes human beings to grow from the earth as a plant; this directly grounds the section's reading of cultivating the nafs as cultivating a field.
terra: After people are grown from earth like plants, they are returned into it and brought out again, distinguishing fruitful burial from the section's suffocating dassa.
terra: Allah makes earth a broad carpet for people, paralleling the section's spread floor and its low vegetation described as carpeting the surface.
terra: Remaining upright is joined to being given abundant water, an indirect moral counterpart to the section's cultivated soul receiving ample irrigation.
terra: The abundant water is itself a test, while turning from the Lord's reminder leads to severe punishment; provision therefore does not by itself prove inner fertility.
terra: The righteous make a spring gush abundantly, preserving the fajara branch's image of opening a controllable path for water in a different setting.
terra: Abundant pouring water descends from rainclouds, repeating the section's image of water coming through the field's ceiling.
terra: Grain and vegetation are brought out by that poured water, a compact parallel to the Abasa sequence of water, split soil, and growth.
terra: Dense gardens complete the rain-to-growth sequence and show the mature abundance toward which the section's tarbiya proceeds.
terra: Moses asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, an invitation to the growth that the section sets against the buried and barren soul.

luna: The source section describes earth's surface as spread for plant life; this verse says earth was spread out, preparing the water and pasture named in 79:31. | terra: Earth is spread out and then furnished for life, directly recalling the section's spread ground as the surface of a field.

luna: The source section's soil is opened to water and growth; this verse names water and pasture brought from the spread earth. | terra: Water and pasture are brought out from that spread earth, making the surface productive in the same sequence the section develops.
terra: Water and pasture are expressly provision for people and livestock, completing the spread-earth scene as sustenance.
terra: The possibility that the blind seeker may purify himself treats moral reception as growth, resonating with the later field sequence in the same surah.
terra: The warning that the dismissive hearer may not purify himself clarifies the receptive boundary around the possible purification named in 80:3.
terra: The command that the human look at his food frames 80:25-32 as a lesson in how a field's nourishment is made, not merely a list of crops.

luna: The source section's field opens with rain from above; here water is poured abundantly before the ground is split and planted, making rain the first condition of growth. | terra: The ayah's emphatic pouring of water is the first exact step in the section's field sequence: the field and the soul receive growth from above.

luna: The source section explicitly glosses its root ف ل ح through ploughing and splitting earth; this verse names the ground being split, the soil-work behind the image. | terra: The earth is explicitly split open, matching both the section's ploughing sense of falaha and its water-opening sense of fajara.

luna: The source section's ploughing and ز ك و as crop growth become concrete in the grain that sprouts from the opened earth. | terra: Grain is made to grow from the opened earth, completing the section's water-splitting-growth sequence and making zakkaha perceptible as cultivation.
terra: Grapes and herbage continue the produce emerging from the split ground, showing the variety hidden in the section's single verb of growth.
terra: Olives and palms extend the field sequence to trees, including the palm whose crown the section's secondary sense of aqr can cut away.
terra: Dense gardens show the mature enclosure formed by water, split earth, and growth in the preceding ayat.
terra: Fruit and pasture identify the yield of the cultivated earth for both human food and grazing.
terra: The produce is provision for people and livestock, completing the field image as divinely apportioned sustenance.
luna: The source section recalls burying a girl in earth as the opposite of growth; this verse's الموءودة is the buried-alive girl, a repeated Qur'anic formulation of that scene.
luna: The source section evokes the buried girl in 16:59; after this verse's buried-alive girl, this ayah asks what sin she was killed for, stating the moral wrong in that parallel.

luna: The source section uses the sky as rain and the ground as a field; this verse calls the sky returning rain, completing the natural condition for the earth's split in 86:12. | terra: The oath by the sky that returns rain names the repeatedly supplied water above the field whose opening is named in 86:12.

luna: The source section's land is opened to water and growth; this verse names earth with a split, alongside the rain-bearing sky in 86:11. | terra: The oath by earth that cracks open gives a terse Quranic counterpart to the section's ploughed soil, opened watercourse, and emerging growth.
terra: The command to glorify the name of the Most High Lord introduces 87:2-5, where Rabb's creating, measuring, guiding, and bringing out pasture enact the section's nurture.
terra: The Lord creates and proportions, supplying the ordered formation that precedes the pasture's growth and the soul's purification.
terra: The Lord measures and guides, making gradual, directed development the bridge from creation to the pasture brought out in 87:4.

luna: The source section's field is a place of spreading plant life; this verse says God brings out pasture from earth. | terra: The Lord brings out pasture, showing Rabb as the one who causes vegetation to emerge and begins its measured nurture.

luna: The source section contrasts flourishing soil with barren sand; the pasture is then made dry, dark stubble, the field's reverse. | terra: The pasture the Lord brings out becomes dark stubble, bounding the image of growth with its withering end.

luna: The source section glosses ز ك و as a crop's growth and links it to cleansing the self; this verse joins success with تزكى, preserving both moral purification and the growth sense. | terra: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ restates both key terms of 91:9, making success and purification/growth an explicit pair.
terra: The command to look at how earth is spread makes the prepared horizontal surface itself an object of reflection, one component of the section's field-house.
terra: The giver spends wealth seeking to purify or increase himself, preserving the section's link between expenditure and the growing soul.
